<reason>Both sides debated tightly and stayed on the motion, with clean Q/A formatting on both ends and clipped turns costing each side a sentence of payoff. CON built the more inventive negative architecture: disclosure only earns scarce shelf-edge attention if it differentiates options; the flag is backward-looking and expires while the shrink is permanent; the drafting trigger is either an escape hatch or a noise generator; and stigmatising the auditable deception pushes firms toward unmeasurable quality degradation. PRO, however, answered the most damaging of these directly rather than deflecting. The expiry attack was neutralised cleanly ("twelve months of being told versus zero days" — an honest sticker rise is visible as a rise for one day and nobody calls that certification). The escape-hatch dilemma was closed with a plausible, non-brittle mechanism (successor mapping retailers already perform for shelf slots, sales history and "buy again"), plus the concession-embracing move that false positives are simply true statements. And PRO's proves-too-much reply to substitution was strong: CON conceded shrinking is chosen because it is the cheapest deception, which is precisely why raising its cost has bite — "the disguise is the confession." CON's own case also carries an unresolved tension PRO partly exposed: if the flag is pure undifferentiating noise that steers no purchase, it cannot simultaneously function as a stigma tax strong enough to flip firms to reformulation. CON's counterplan (bigger, consistent unit prices) is also a partial concession to the motion's clarity aim, and PRO landed the neat turn that CON's remedy relies on the very number CON says the anchored shopper ignores. CON's uniform-shrink noise point survives as a real cost, but PRO retains the conceded premise (a shrunken box is a price rise) plus low-cost implementation and an unrefuted market-discipline mechanism, giving the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]/[B4.1] turn — "you cannot say shoppers don't read the tag as your problem and putting it on the tag as your solution," refined into the anchor-versus-annotation distinction — was the sharpest single strike. But PRO's counter-turn in [A5.2]-[A5.3] blunted it: CON's own remedy (a bigger unit price) depends on attention to the figure CON says she skips, while the flag can sit inside the price she does read, and firms would not retool moulds to protect a sticker no one consults.</best_rebuttal>
